There is a sentence I hear from every senior person who works in a second language, and it is always the same sentence. In my own language I am a director, and in English I sound like somebody's assistant. That is not vanity. It is accurate, and it is not about grammar. Authority in a meeting is carried almost entirely by delivery, by pace, by where the pauses fall, by whether you finish your own sentences. In a second language all of that goes first, long before the vocabulary does. The word arrives late, the sentence trails off, and the room quietly gives the floor to somebody else. Nobody decides to do it. It simply happens. So what I tell people is to stop trying to be faster. Speed is not the thing you lost. Work on holding the floor while you are slow, because that is the part the room is actually reading.

For years I had one move when a word did not come, and it was to apologise. Sorry, my English. I said it perhaps four times a call, and I thought it was modesty. It was not. Every one of those apologies told the room to lower its expectations of me, and rooms do what they are told. What I have now is three sentences and nothing else. Let me put that a different way. The short answer is yes, and I will come back to the detail. And, when I genuinely have nothing, that is a fair question, give me a second on it. I used to think a phrase like that was filler. It is not filler, it is furniture. It holds the space up while I find the word. And the Spanish still arrives first, most days. It just does not get to finish the sentence any more.
